Issued at 1121 PM CDT Fri Aug 28 2026

Lee of the Black Hills surface low and a tight gradient in place to 
the east of it has led to a strengthening 30-40kt low level jet over 
eastern SD (near and east of the James River Valley). KABR VAD 
profile has highlighted that increasing LLVL jet since around 01Z. 
As that started to develop, the convection increased in portions of 
east-central SD and expect that to be the main driver of the severe 
threat through the early morning hours. Based on the SPC MesoA data, 
the best WAA focuses farther to the southeast and into southeastern 
SD, so may see the storms trend that direction with time. That 
matches up with the latest 02Z HRRR run, keeping storm threat in 
east-central and southeast SD. Severe hail/winds are possible with 
any storms tonight, especially hail initially before storms move 
eastward and into lower instability (drops from 2.5k J/kg MUCAPE to 
1-1.25k over eastern SD). If there is any organization, wind would 
become a greater threat. The storms should move out of the area 
between 4-7am. Finally, any storm may produce heavy rain, as PWAT 
values are 160% of normal on the 00Z KABR sounding and storm motions 
are around 25 mph. 

Behind this morning's convection, expect a lull across most of the 
area, as the low level jet veers to the WSW and focuses into MN and 
the temp advection follows suit (as the surface low shifts into NE). 
Still have enough mid-upper level moisture moving across the area 
(as seen on upstream WV imagery across the mountain west) to lead to 
a partly cloudy sky. Models even hint at some short wave energy 
trying to move through and that likely is why a few models are 
showing some weak returns across northern SD towards late morning 
and into the afternoon. With bases up around 12-15kft and fairly dry 
air sub-cloud, didn't include any PoPs, but did add some sprinkle 
mention to the northern counties as that slides through. 

Later this afternoon and evening, confidence is low on thunderstorm 
potential and location. This is due to the weakening low level flow 
around the broad/weak low over the area (northeast winds <15kts from 
sfc-850mb) and likely becoming re-established near the Black Hills. 
That low level flow and low location leads to the Black Hills and 
maybe areas to the north of that being the best chance for initial 
development, but could even see an isolated storm develop between 
the Black Hills and the Missouri River if there is some local 
convergence. Once development occurs, storms will move off to the 
east-northeast around 20kts and move into a little better 
instability (2-2.5k J/kg in central SD in the evening). Shear 
remains the same (30-40kts) across the area, so would expect the 
severe potential to continue as storms move into central SD from the 
west through the evening. These storms have the potential to produce 
1"+ hail and 60mph winds, but would expect an eventual transition to 
primarily a wind threat and weakening as storms move into a less 
favorable in eastern SD (or dive south into the better instability). 
One area of a very conditional threat is if storms develop near the 
ND/SD border west of Lemmon towards evening. This would be an area 
of increased shear (40-50kts) and SRH (100-150 of 0-3km), 
potentially being a favorable environment for supercell 
characteristics and hail up to 2" with the elongated and straight 
hodographs. One last thing to watch for tonight is a warm front 
stretching east across east-central SD. Confidence is low overall, 
as the low level jet isn't as strong (5-15kts), which leads to more 
broad/weak WAA in that area. So potential for development is 
present, but also low chances (10-20%) at this point. 

For Sunday, the upper low moves from the northwest MT and Canada 
border on Sunday morning to southern Saskatchewan by Monday morning. 
With that track, the best upper level support (q-vect conv) tracks 
across the northwest half of ND and potentially brushes our north 
central. That being said, we do have the persistent surface low over 
central SD and potential warm front stretching east across northeast 
SD and a cold front south across the south central. This provides 
sources of lift and with 1500-2500 J/kg of CAPE and 40-45kts of 
shear, thus a severe potential remains. Looking closer at forecast 
soundings, there does appear to be some low-moderate CIN (-50-125 
J/kg), which may keep the potential for development in our area to 
be more isolated. That matches up with the regional/global models, 
which point towards the better chance of storms being tied to 
upstream convection that may move into the northern parts of the 
CWA. With storm motions to the east to east-northeast and large 
scale forcing lifting northeast, will need to monitor expectations 
farther to our west and see how they evolve over the next couple 
days and influence our severe potential.
